content: The use of male circumcision (MC) devices in individuals under the age of 18 is not recommended due to insufficient data on safety and efficacy in this age group. Furthermore, given the limited evidence regarding the safety of MC devices in men living with HIV, it is critical to closely monitor their use in this population to ensure safety and minimize potential risks. The risk of HIV transmission during the wound-healing period following circumcision should be evaluated through modeling studies. This approach will provide a clearer understanding of the risk-benefit balance and inform the development of effective client education and counseling strategies at service delivery sites. Since the complete healing process, including scar maturation and remodeling, can take up to one year after circumcision, it is essential to compare the cosmetic and functional outcomes of device-based circumcision with those achieved through conventional surgical methods at the one-year mark. The integration of device-based circumcision methods into existing MC programs is likely to result in a mixed-method service delivery model rather than a single-method approach. As countries continue to scale up MC programs, it is important to assess the incremental costs associated with introducing device-based circumcision, considering the diverse settings in which these services are delivered. Additionally, it is necessary to study the impact of introducing MC devices on the demand for medical circumcision services. Changes in demand, whether an increase or decrease, can significantly influence the overall cost-effectiveness of these programs. Finally, ongoing research and evaluation are required to ensure that the implementation of MC devices aligns with safety, efficacy, and cost-effectiveness goals, while also addressing the unique needs of different populations and healthcare settings.
